nameStory: The 'silver' in this spider's name comes from its distinctive metallic silvery sheen that catches light like a tiny mirror. The 'long-jawed' part refers to the prominent, elongated mouthparts (chelicerae) that extend forward like tweezers. These impressive 'jaws' are especially noticeable when the spider is at rest, stretched out along a blade of grass or twig.
description: The Silver Long-jawed Orbweaver is a slender, elegant spider with a distinctive silvery appearance that shimmers in sunlight. Like other stretch spiders, it has an elongated body and extremely long legs that it uses to stretch out in a perfectly straight line when hiding. These spiders build horizontal orb webs, usually close to water, and are most active during dawn and dusk hours. They're medium-sized spiders that blend remarkably well with their surroundings when motionless.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely elongated, narrow body with long, thin legs that can stretch out in a perfectly straight line along grass stems or twigs

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Distinctive silvery metallic sheen on the abdomen that reflects light like polished metal, often with subtle darker patterns underneath

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Horizontal orb web that feels sticky to the touch, typically built low to the ground near water sources or damp areas

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Most active at dawn and dusk (crepuscular), often seen stretched motionless along plant stems during the day in perfect camouflage

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Two rows of four eyes each, with the front row eyes appearing larger and more prominent when viewed head-on

habitat: Found near wetlands, pond edges, marshes, and stream banks throughout New England, always close to water sources. They prefer areas with tall grasses, cattails, and other vertical vegetation where they can build their horizontal webs. Look for them in the transition zones between water and upland areas, especially where morning dew lingers longest.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging and can be found building webs near water sources. Look for their silvery shimmer on dewy mornings when they're most visible.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with fully mature adults active at dawn and dusk. Mating occurs during nighttime hours, so pairs may be spotted together on webs.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue to be active through early fall, with egg-laying occurring. Spiders may be found stretched along dried grass stems and seed heads.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically don't survive freezing temperatures, but egg sacs overwinter to produce next year's generation.

funFact: These spiders go through an incredible nine different growth stages (instars) before reaching adulthood - that means they molt their entire skin eight times, getting bigger and more silvery with each transformation!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Green Long-jawed Orbweaver, but the Silver has that distinctive metallic silvery shine while the Green species appears more yellow-green. Memory trick: 'Silver shimmers, Green is plain' - the metallic reflection is the giveaway.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'long-jawed' can be misleading since these aren't actually jaws like mammals have, but rather specialized mouthparts called chelicerae that contain the fangs. The 'orbweaver' name refers to their circular web pattern, though this species builds horizontal rather than vertical orb webs.
compareHints: Among the Tetragnatha genus in New England, the Silver Long-jawed Orbweaver stands out for its distinctive metallic silvery appearance, while the Green Long-jawed Orbweaver appears more yellow-green and the Common Stretch Spider tends to be brownish. All share the same elongated body plan and stretching behavior, but the Silver's reflective sheen makes it the easiest to distinguish when present.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Tetragnatha relatives, the Green Long-jawed Orbweaver stands out with its vivid green coloration, while the Common Stretch Spider tends to be more yellowish or brownish, and the Silver Long-jawed Orbweaver has distinctive metallic silver markings.
Among New England's long-jawed orbweavers, the Common Stretch Spider is distinguished by its extreme elongation and distinctive straight-line defensive posture.
Among its stretch spider relatives, the Elongate Stilt Spider has the most extreme body elongation - much more stretched than the Common Stretch Spider or Green Long-jawed Orbweaver.
Unlike the Green Long-jawed Orbweaver that stays near water and has greenish coloring, versicolor prefers dry areas and shows yellow-orange tones.
Compared to its relatives, the Straw-colored Stretch Spider is consistently paler than the bright green T.
Unlike the Common Stretch Spider which has a more uniform abdomen, the tailed long-jawed orbweaver has that distinctive rear projection.
